title: As-Sami' and al-Basir
hook: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, who hears whispers and sees the ant

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing, who knows what the heart hides. Your line was he already knows. Did you tell him the thing you'd told no one? Day two hundred forty-eight.

A woman in Medina has a problem at home, and it's a bad one. Her husband has said an old Arabian oath that leaves her neither married nor free. She comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and she argues. She pleads. She complains, out loud, to God. His wife Aisha is in the same room, and she said later that she could not even hear all of what the woman was saying. It was that low, that close. And then verses came down that begin: God has heard the words of the woman who argued with you about her husband. The person in the room missed some of it. The one she was really talking to missed none of it. Today, two names that go together: the One who hears, and the One who sees.
screen: `A WOMAN ARGUES HER CASE.` → `AISHA CAN'T HEAR IT ALL.` → `GOD HAS HEARD.`

segments.voice: As-Sami': the All-Hearing, from sam', hearing. Al-Basir: the All-Seeing, from basar, sight. In the Qur'an they very often come as a pair, at the end of a verse, like two notes of one chord. One verse puts it this way, in Pickthall's old translation: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Notice what that line does. First it says nothing is like him. Then it uses two words we use about ourselves. Muslim scholars read it as a guard rail: God hears and sees, truly, but not with ears and eyes like ours, and not the way we do. Our hearing gets tired. His doesn't. Our sight needs light. His doesn't. There's a saying often repeated in Muslim teaching, that God sees a black ant on a black stone on a moonless night. It's a picture, not a verse, but it makes the point: nothing is too small or too dark. And the pair isn't only about being watched. When Moses and Aaron are sent to face Pharaoh, they're afraid, and God tells them not to fear: "Lo! I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing." That's comfort, not surveillance. The woman in Medina is the same lesson told as a story. She had no lawyer, no power, no loud voice. She had a complaint whispered in a corner, and the chapter she's remembered in is named for her: al-Mujadilah, the woman who argues. The Prophet taught that when people call on God, they're not calling someone deaf or far away. Heard. Seen. Even the whisper.
screen: `SAMI' — HEARING. BASIR — SEEING.` · `NOTHING IS LIKE HIM.` · `I AM WITH YOU, HEARING AND SEEING.` · `THE WOMAN WHO ARGUES.` · then, large: `HEARD. SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: whisper a du'a. Sit, and let the room go quiet. Think of one thing you want, or one thing that hurts, and say it so softly nobody near you could catch it. In your own words, in any language. If you pray, you can speak it to God, as quietly as the woman in Medina. If you don't, just let yourself say it at all, and notice how different it feels to say a thing than to only think it. Then sit in the quiet after. The bell holds the time.
As-Sami' and al-Basir. The All-Hearing and the All-Seeing, two names that travel together through the Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: heard, seen. Today, when you feel overlooked, in a meeting, a group chat, a kitchen, say those two words to yourself once. Day two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims call on God as as-Sami' and al-Basir in private du'a, often quietly or silently, and many say after rising from bowing in prayer that God hears the one who praises him.

fork.setup: you're the woman in Medina. your husband's oath has left you stuck. nobody powerful is on your side. what do you do?
options: say nothing and put up with it.
bring your case to the Prophet and complain to God.
fork.reveal: she argued and complained to God, so quietly Aisha missed some of it, and a whole surah opens with God has heard her.

original.note: Arabic: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. from sam' (hearing) and basar (sight).

trapdoor: what you thought: God is watching you.
what it means: nothing is too quiet to be heard or too small to be seen, and the Qur'an mostly says it as comfort.
what a scholar hears: 42:11 sets the two names right after naught is as His likeness, so they're affirmed without picturing ears or eyes like ours.

sources.quoted: Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer.

sources.ref: Qur'an 58:1 (God has heard the woman who disputed with you about her husband)
Aisha's report that she could not hear all of Khawlah's words (Sunan Ibn Majah 188; Sunan an-Nasa'i 3460; cited by al-Bukhari in Kitab at-Tawhid)
hadith: you are not calling one who is deaf or absent (Sahih al-Bukhari 2992)
